units.title: Basics 1
units.description: Learn your very first Korean words and sentences! Meet people, name foods, and start talking about what you eat and drink.
units.guidebook:
# Welcome to Basics 1! 🇰🇷

Korean sentences often drop the subject because the verb ending tells you who's doing what. The verb **이다** (to be) is rarely used alone — instead, adjectives and descriptive verbs attach **-이에요/예요** for "is/am/are."

**Particles** are small markers after nouns:
- **은/는** = topic marker ("as for…")
- **이/가** = subject marker ("…is the one")

**To eat** = **먹다** → **먹어요** (eats / I eat)
**To drink** = **마시다** → **마셔요** (drinks / I drink)

**Word order:** Subject + Object + Verb. Example: "I eat bread" → **저는 빵을 먹어요** (jeo-neun ppang-eul meo-geo-yo). The object marker **을/를** marks what is eaten or drunk.

**Politeness:** **-요** endings are polite but friendly — perfect for beginners!

exercises.answer: I am a woman.
I am a girl.
I eat bread.
I drink milk.

units.title: Greetings
units.description: Learn essential Korean greetings and polite expressions for everyday interactions.
units.guidebook:
## Greetings in Korean

Korean greetings often depend on **formality** and **social context**. The most common greeting is **안녕하세요** (annyeonghaseyo), a polite "hello" used in most situations.

### Saying Hello & Goodbye
- **안녕하세요** — the standard polite hello, used any time of day.
- **안녕** (annyeong) is informal, used with close friends or younger people.
- **잘 가요** (jal gayo) means "goodbye" when *you* are staying.
- **안녕히 가세요** (annyeonghi gaseyo) is a more respectful "goodbye" to someone leaving.

### Morning & Night
- **좋은 아침입니다** (joeun achimimnida) — "Good morning" (formal).
- **좋은 저녁입니다** — "Good evening."
- **안녕히 주무세요** — "Good night" (to someone going to sleep).

### Politeness Basics
- **감사합니다** (gamsahamnida) — "Thank you" (formal).
- **고마워요** (gomawoyo) — "Thank you" (polite but casual).
- **죄송합니다** (joesonghamnida) — "I'm sorry" (formal).
- **괜찮아요** (gwaenchanayo) — "It's okay / I'm fine."

### How Are You?
- **잘 지내세요?** (jal jinaeseyo?) — "How are you?" (polite).
- A common reply: **네, 잘 지내요** (ne, jal jinaeyo) — "Yes, I'm doing well."

💡 **Tip:** When in doubt, use **-요** endings — they're polite but friendly!

exercises.answer: Yes, I am doing well.
Good morning.
Good night.

exercises.prompt: 죄송합니다, 다시 한 번 말해 주세요.
exercises.audioTarget: 죄송합니다, 다시 한 번 말해 주세요.

exercises.prompt: 죄송합니다, 다시 한 번 말해 주세요.
exercises.audioTarget: 죄송합니다, 다시 한 번 말해 주세요.

units.title: Food
units.description: Learn essential food and drink vocabulary in Korean, plus how to say what you want, eat, and drink.
units.guidebook:
## Talking About Food in Korean 🍚

Korean has no separate word for "a" or "the" — context tells you which is meant. So **밥** (*bap*) can mean "rice," "the rice," or just "a meal."

**Saying what you want:** Use **~을/를 주세요** (*~eul/reul juseyo*), meaning "please give me~". Pick **을** after a consonant (밥을) and **를** after a vowel (커피를). Example: **커피를 주세요** — "Coffee, please."

**Saying you eat/drink:** Use **먹어요** (*meogeoyo*, "eat") and **마셔요** (*masyeoyo*, "drink"). Both end in **-어요**, the friendly present tense ending.

- **저는 밥을 먹어요** — "I eat rice."
- **저는 물을 마셔요** — "I drink water."

**Topic marker:** **저는** (*jeoneun*) means "as for me / I." The **는** highlights the topic of your sentence.

**Quick tip:** 🥚 계란 and 달걀 both mean "egg" — 계란 is more common in everyday speech. Practice ordering: "**저는 ___ 주세요**" works for almost any food or drink!

exercises.answer: I drink coffee.
Water, please.
I drink tea.
I drink milk.

units.title: Animals
units.description: Learn the names of common animals in Korean and how to describe them with simple sentences.
units.guidebook:
# Animals 🐾

Welcome to the Animals unit! In this lesson, you'll learn the names of common animals in Korean and how to make simple sentences about them.

## Topic Marker

In Korean, the particle **은/는** is used to mark the topic of a sentence. Use **는** after a vowel and **은** after a consonant.

- 개**는** (gae-neun) — *as for the dog*
- 말**은** (ma-reun) — *as for the horse*

## Descriptive Verb: ~이다 (to be)

To say "X is Y," use the pattern: **Noun + 은/는 + Noun + 이에요/예요**.

- Use **이에요** after a consonant: 개는 강아지**예요** (The dog is a puppy).
- Use **예요** after a vowel: 새는 예뻐요 (The bird is pretty).

## Plural Marker

Korean doesn't always mark plurals, but you can add **들** to make a noun plural:

- 물고기 → 물고기**들** (fish → fishes)

## Sentence Endings

**~이에요/예요** is the polite informal ending, perfect for beginners. Try combining animal names with descriptive verbs like **예뻐요** (is pretty), **커요** (is big), and **좋아요** (is good).

exercises.answer: The cat is small.
The bird flies in the sky.

exercises.translation: The fish lives in the water.

exercises.answer: The cow gives milk.
The tiger is scary.

units.title: Travel
units.description: Learn essential Korean vocabulary and phrases for getting around cities, using transportation, staying at hotels, and finding places.
units.guidebook:
## Getting Around in Korean

This unit covers essential travel vocabulary. Korean uses **postpositional particles** that come after nouns to show their role in a sentence.

**Key particles to know:**
- **은/는** (eun/neun) — topic marker: "as for..."
- **이/가** (i/ga) — subject marker: identifies the doer
- **을/를** (eul/reul) — object marker: marks what receives the action
- **에** (e) — location or time marker: "at/in/to"
- **에서** (eseo) — "at/from (a place)"

**Asking where things are:**
Use **어디에 있어요?** (eodi-e isseoyo?) — "Where is it?"
Pattern: **Noun + 에 + 있어요** — "It is at [place]."
Example: **호텔에 있어요** (hotel-e isseoyo) — "It is at the hotel."

**Getting around:**
- **~에 가다** (e gada) — "to go to~"
- **~에서 ~까지** (eseo ~ kkaji) — "from ~ to~"

**Politeness:** All phrases use **-요** (-yo) style, the standard polite speech suitable for travelers. Keep practicing — you're doing great!

exercises.answer: I am going to the hotel.
The subway station is over there.

exercises.translation: I want to go to the museum.

exercises.answer: I take the train from Seoul to Busan.
Is there a hotel near here?

units.title: Family
units.description: Learn words for family members and describe your household in Korean.
units.guidebook:
### Talking About Family in Korean

Family terms in Korean vary depending on who is speaking:

- **If you are male:** Call an older brother **형** (*hyeong*) and an older sister **누나** (*nuna*).
- **If you are female:** Call an older brother **오빠** (*oppa*) and an older sister **언니** (*eonni*).

For a younger sibling, regardless of gender, use **동생** (*dongsaeng*). To specify, you can say **남동생** (*younger brother*) or **여동생** (*younger sister*).

### Respect and Politeness

Koreans often use honorific titles. For parents, **부모님** (*bumonim*) includes the polite suffix **-님** (*-nim*). When referring to your own family to others, use **우리** (*uri*, literally "our") instead of "my"—for example, **우리 가족** (*our family*).

exercises.translation: There are four people in our family.

exercises.answer: Mother is good at cooking.
Grandfather takes a walk in the park.
The baby is sleeping in the room.

exercises.translation: My younger sibling is a student.

exercises.answer: My older brother is not home right now.

units.title: Shopping
units.description: Learn how to ask for prices, navigate stores, and buy items in Korean.
units.guidebook:
### Essential Shopping Phrases

When shopping in Korea, asking for prices is simple! Just point and ask:
* **이거 얼마예요?** (*Igeo eolmayeyo?*) — "How much is this?"

### Payment Methods with -(으)로
To indicate your payment method, attach the particle **-(으)로** ("by" or "with"):
* **카드로** (*kadeuro*) — "by card"
* **현금으로** (*hyeongeum-euro*) — "with cash"
Pair it with **계산해 주세요** (*gyesanhae juseyo*, "please charge/check out").

### Cheap vs. Expensive
* **비싸요** (*bissayo*) = "It is expensive."
* **싸요** (*ssayo*) = "It is cheap."

Add **너무** (*neomu*, "too") when something exceeds your budget: **너무 비싸요** (*neomu bissayo*, "It's too expensive!").

exercises.answer: This T-shirt is really cheap.
I buy fruit at the market.

exercises.translation: I'd like to pay by card, please.

exercises.answer: Can I pay with cash?
I bought shoes at the department store.

units.title: Weather
units.description: Talk about the weather, seasons, and daily conditions in Korean.
units.guidebook:
### Talking About the Weather

In Korean, talking about precipitation is easy! Instead of saying 'it rains,' Koreans say that rain or snow 'comes':
- **비가 와요** (*Biga wayo*) = It is raining (literally, 'rain comes').
- **눈이 와요** (*Nuni wayo*) = It is snowing ('snow comes').

### ㅂ-Irregular Adjectives
Weather adjectives like **덥다** (*deopda*, to be hot) and **춥다** (*chupda*, to be cold) are irregular. When conjugated into the polite present tense, the **ㅂ** changes to **우**, resulting in:
- 덥다 → **더워요** (*deowoyo*)
- 춥다 → **추워요** (*chuwoyo*)

### Seasons with Time Particle -에
Add the time particle **-에** (*-e*) to seasons to mean 'in': **여름에** (*in summer*), **겨울에** (*in winter*).

exercises.translation: The weather is really nice today.

exercises.answer: It is raining a lot outside.

exercises.translation: In winter, the weather is very cold.

exercises.answer: In summer, the weather is too hot.

exercises.translation: The wind blows a lot today.

exercises.answer: There are really many clouds in the sky.
Warm wind blows in the spring.

units.title: Work & School
units.description: Learn essential vocabulary for professions, school life, and office environments in Korean.
units.guidebook:
Welcome to **Work & School**! Here are two essential grammar tips for this unit:

### 1. Locations: -에 vs. -에서
Both particles indicate locations, but in different ways:
- Use **-에** with movement verbs like `가다` (to go) or existence verbs like `있다` (to be/exist): *학교에 가요* ("I go to school").
- Use **-에서** when a specific action happens at a location: *사무실에서 일해요* ("I work at the office").

### 2. Respectful Suffix: -님
In Korean, respecting professionals and seniors is vital. The suffix **-님** (nim) attaches to professions to show politeness, turning *선생* into *선생님* (teacher). Always address teachers with this honorific!

exercises.answer: The doctor works at the hospital.
Today's class is very interesting.
I work together with my colleague.

exercises.translation: There is a book on the desk.

exercises.answer: I go to school early tomorrow.

units.title: Health
units.description: Talk about body parts, express symptoms, and navigate visits to the doctor or pharmacy.
units.guidebook:
### Talking About Symptoms

To say that a body part hurts, attach the subject particle **-이/가** to the body part followed by **아파요** (hurts/is sick):
* **머리가 아파요.** (My head hurts / I have a headache.)
* **배가 아파요.** (My stomach hurts.)

### Taking Medicine in Korean
In English, we say "take medicine," but in Korean, you literally *eat* medicine using the verb **먹다**:
* **약을 먹어요.** (I take medicine.)

### Catching a Cold
To express that you have caught an illness like a cold, use the idiom **감기에 걸리다**:
* **감기에 걸렸어요.** (I caught a cold.)

When resting, Koreans often say **푹 쉬세요** (Please rest well).

exercises.answer: Wash your hands cleanly.
I caught a cold, so I go to the hospital.
My stomach hurt, so I went to the pharmacy.
My eyes hurt a little.
